```{r setup}
library(sdidlab)
panel <- prop99_panel()
```

## Why placebo inference

Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) offer three variance estimators for SDID:
bootstrap, jackknife and placebo. With a single treated unit, the bootstrap
and the jackknife both need to resample or drop the treated unit, so they are
undefined, and the placebo variance is the one that applies. It assigns
treatment to control units at random, re-estimates the effect each time, and
uses the spread of those placebo effects as the standard error.

sdidlab computes it exactly as synthdid does. With trimming off
(`trim_k = Inf`), the result is `sqrt(vcov(est, method = "placebo"))` from
synthdid, draw for draw under the same seed:

```{r}
setup <- build_setup(sdid_spec(), panel)
est <- synthdid::synthdid_estimate(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0)

set.seed(42); theirs <- sqrt(vcov(est, method = "placebo", replications = 100))
set.seed(42); mine <- placebo_se_trimmed(est, replications = 100, trim_k = Inf)$se
c(synthdid = as.numeric(theirs), sdidlab = mine)
```

## Why trim

The placebo standard error treats every control as a stand-in for the treated
unit. In a large, heterogeneous donor pool, many controls look nothing like
the treated unit: the estimator cannot fit their pre-period, so their placebo
"effects" are large for reasons unrelated to uncertainty about the treated
unit's effect. Those draws fatten the tails of the reference distribution and
inflate the standard error.

`placebo_se_trimmed()` drops placebos whose pre-period fit is more than
`trim_k` times worse than the treated unit's. This is in the spirit of Abadie,
Diamond and Hainmueller (2010), who exclude placebos with poor pre-treatment
fit from their permutation test. Two design points matter:

* **It trims the inference distribution, not the donor pool.** The
  counterfactual is still built from every donor, and the point estimate is
  unchanged.
* **The criterion is pre-treatment fit, decided in advance.** Fit is measured
  without reference to any unit's estimated effect, so trimming cannot be
  tuned to produce a preferred answer as long as `trim_k` is fixed beforehand.

Fit is measured as the RMSE of the treated-minus-synthetic gap after removing
its pre-period mean, because SDID's unit fixed effects absorb a constant
level difference by design. When covariates are used, it is computed on the
covariate-adjusted outcome the estimator actually fits.

**Trimming is sdidlab's addition, not part of the SDID paper**, and its
statistical properties are not established in the literature. Report the
untrimmed standard error alongside it, and treat a conclusion that holds
under one but not the other as fragile.

## What trimming did here

`plot_placebo_trim()` shows every placebo's pre-period fit and where the
cutoff fell:

```{r}
run <- fit_spec(sdid_spec(inference = list(replications = 200)), panel, seed = 1)
plot_placebo_trim(run)
```

```{r}
untrimmed <- fit_spec(sdid_spec(inference = list(replications = 200, trim_k = Inf)), panel, seed = 1)
data.frame(
  trim_k = c("Inf (synthdid)", "5"),
  se = c(untrimmed$fit$se, run$fit$se),
  placebos_kept = c(untrimmed$fit$placebos_kept, run$fit$placebos_kept)
)
```

The 38 Proposition 99 donors are fairly homogeneous, so trimming changes the
standard error only modestly here. It matters most in pools of hundreds of
units with very different trajectories.

## Checking calibration with in-time placebos

A standard error can be checked against a case where the true effect is known
to be zero. Move the treatment date back into the pre-period, fit only on
pre-1989 data, and see how often the resulting |t| is large. A calibrated
standard error gives |t| < 1.96 about 95% of the time. With only a handful of
fake dates this is a sanity check, not a test:

```{r}
fake_years <- 1980:1986
calib <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fake_years, function(y) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c(Inf, 5), function(k) {
    spec <- sdid_spec(design = list(treat_time = y, window = list(end = 1988)),
                      inference = list(replications = 100, trim_k = k))
    r <- fit_spec(spec, panel, seed = seed_for(spec))
    data.frame(fake_year = y, trim_k = k, att = r$fit$att, se = r$fit$se, t = r$fit$t)
  }))
}))
calib$t <- round(calib$t, 2)
calib
```

With trimming, a large |t| on in-time placebos would be a warning that the
trimmed standard error is too small. Running this check on your own panel is
the best guide to whether trimming is appropriate there.

## Which donors drive the standard error

`donor_influence()` splits the placebo variance by the control that stood in
for the treated unit in each draw, and sets it against that control's weight
in the counterfactual:

```{r}
plot_donor_influence(run)
```

A donor far above the diagonal adds more uncertainty than it contributes to
the estimate. Dropping donors *because* they raise the standard error is
selection on the result. The figure is for understanding an interval, not for
choosing a pool.
